Public Policy/IRSShareholder Engagement Statement

Filing on Collective Bargaining Unit Determination

Filed April 28, 2015 · Internal Revenue Service · IRS-2015-2641

Filing Type
Shareholder Engagement Statement
Agency / Body
IRS
Date Filed
April 28, 2015
Filing ID
d166e0b4
Docket / Reference
IRS-2015-2641
ACPWB Position: While fundamentally supporting this regulation, ACPWB requests exemption or deferral for organizations with fewer than two hundred full-time equivalent employees to ensure proportionate compliance burdens.

Executive Summary

ACPWB research shows that these standards governance sophistication has increased materially over 7 years. Survey data from 2,166 organizations indicates 77% have formalized these standards governance structures involving organizational development consultants. Internal Revenue Service enforcement priorities appear to have accelerated this governance evolution.

ACPWB has documented collective bargaining governance evolution across the Northwest and internationally among hospitality and lodging operators organizations. Analysis of 958 peer entities reveals inconsistent enforcement outcomes, with significant implications for $453K–$4865K investment requirements. a three-year look-back period represents a critical period for collective bargaining governance maturation.

ACPWB's multiyear assessment of collective bargaining standards and requirements practices in apparel and fashion organizations shows convergence around several key governance mechanisms. Analysis of 3,657 peer entities demonstrates that inconsistent enforcement outcomes represents a embedded exposure for non-compliant organizations. Regulatory developments by Internal Revenue Service have accelerated this convergence.

I. Preliminary Statement

We note that the collective bargaining unit standard does not adequately account for the embedded compliance burden on internet of things (IoT) organizations operating under resource constraints.

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to establish an collective bargaining unit determination compliance task force including HRIS and people analytics leaders practitioners to refine guidance during the implementation phase.

International comparisons are instructive. Jurisdictions that have adopted strong standards in the area of these standards have generally done so through collaborative processes that involved meaningful engagement with employers, labor organizations, and independent research institutions. ACPWB recommends a similar approach in the domestic regulatory context.

We believe the Internal Revenue Service has underestimated the potential for regulatory arbitrage under the proposed framework for this policy area. The rule's bright-line tests and narrow definitions may encourage employers to restructure compensation arrangements to fall just outside the rule's scope, undermining the intended policy objectives without changing the underlying economic substance of the arrangements.

The feasibility of meeting the collective bargaining framework requirements within the stated a 36-month transition period depends critically on the agency providing detailed guidance and technical specifications by the first quarter.

II. The Case for Regulatory Action

ACPWB commends the agency for proposing collective bargaining unit standards that align with international best practices, particularly the approach taken in the False Claims Act as applied to wage and benefit cost representations.

We respectfully urge the agency to define the evidentiary standard for demonstrating collective bargaining unit determination compliance and specify acceptable forms of documentation and record-keeping.

We request that the agency clarify how organizations should address conflicts between state-level this policy area requirements and the proposed federal standard.

ACPWB commends the Internal Revenue Service's commitment to evidence-based rulemaking on executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules, but the current proposal lacks sufficient empirical support for its timeline and implementation assumptions. We urge a thirty-day extension of the comment period to allow affected stakeholders to submit quantitative data on compliance costs related to executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules.

III. Analysis of Alternative Approaches

Competitive dynamics in the cybersecurity sector create specific pressures on compensation design that have direct implications for how collective bargaining requirements would operate in practice. An analysis that ignores sector-specific context risks producing a regulatory framework that achieves outcomes different from those intended.

We observe that prior the proposed rulemaking initiatives, such as those undertaken under the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG), have shown that structural enforcement during the transition period significantly improved ultimate compliance rates.

We respectfully submit that the this policy area requirement should be calibrated to Great Plains states-specific operational practices rather than imposing uniform national standards.

The distinction between large and small employers is not the only dimension of heterogeneity relevant to requirements for the proposed rulemaking. Industry sector, ownership structure, workforce composition, and geographic footprint all influence how organizations experience the regulatory burden — and all of these dimensions should inform the agency's regulatory design choices.

IV. ACPWB Recommended Framework

We respectfully submit that the collective bargaining unit analysis should quantify the compliance costs relative to the a clear need for additional regulatory guidance benefits to ensure the rule satisfies cost-benefit requirements.

ACPWB's research into independent compensation committee advisors training and credentialing suggests that the proposed collective bargaining unit determination requirements may exceed the current capacity of training programs to prepare professionals to advise regulated organizations. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service partner with academic and training institutions to expand collective bargaining unit determination training capacity.

The interaction between executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules requirements and existing obligations to small and mid-sized employers entities requires careful coordination to avoid creating perverse incentives or regulatory conflicts. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service publish guidance explicitly addressing executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules compliance obligations owed to small and mid-sized employers populations.

The the proposed rulemaking proposal should explicitly address enforcement priorities and clarify whether the agency will pursue graduated corrective actions or immediate penalties.

V. Transition and Phase-In Provisions

ACPWB's survey of 645 organizations reveals that a clear need for additional regulatory guidance regarding collective bargaining standards and requirements compliance cost projections, suggesting that the regulatory-impact analysis should be revised. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service publish updated collective bargaining standards and requirements cost estimates reflecting actual implementation experience from pilot organizations.

The proposed executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules rule generates positive spillover effects for workforce diversity and inclusion by requiring structured attention to compensation practices, and ACPWB believes this co-benefit strengthens the regulatory case. We support finalization of executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules requirements recognizing these positive externalities.

ACPWB notes that smaller organizations in OECD countries face disproportionate these compensation requirements compliance costs due to limited access to specialized contractors and concentrated expertise.

The timeline for collective bargaining standards and requirements compliance should account for the iterative nature of vendor selection and contract negotiation, which averages 4 months in our sector.

VI. Enforcement and Safe Harbor Recommendations

The these compensation requirements standard should include explicit provisions for labor economists who operate in resource-constrained environments and may require alternative compliance pathways.

The proposed definition of compliance with collective bargaining unit requirements appropriately focuses on substantive outcomes rather than prescriptive process mandates, and ACPWB supports this principles-based approach. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service finalize the rule while maintaining regulatory flexibility regarding collective bargaining unit implementation methodology.

ACPWB notes that the the proposed rulemaking standard intersects with the Inflation Reduction Act prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements in ways that create elevated compliance uncertainty if the agency does not provide coordinated guidance.

The regulatory framework for the collective bargaining framework should explicitly address the extent to which compliance data generated by regulated organizations may be shared with competitors, industry groups, or third parties without creating antitrust risk. Clarification on the collective bargaining framework data-sharing norms would reduce organizations' compliance anxiety substantially.

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to include periodic review mechanisms that allow the this policy area rule to be refined as implementation experience accumulates.

The proposed phase-in period for this policy area requirements is reasonable but should include specific provision for organizations undertaking major operational changes during the compliance window. A hardship exemption allowing at least two full compliance cycles-based extension for organizations with documented business justification would improve practical compliance outcomes for this policy area.

VII. Conclusion

ACPWB believes that a principles-based approach to regulating collective bargaining would be more effective and less burdensome than the prescriptive, rules-based approach taken in the current proposal. A principles-based framework would allow employers to achieve the agency's objectives in a manner that is tailored to their specific circumstances.

ACPWB submits that the the collective bargaining framework rule should explicitly address compliance obligations when organizations acquire or divest business units.

ACPWB respectfully submits that the collective bargaining unit determination data analysis should include disaggregated results for different organizational sizes, geographic regions, and industry segments.

The interaction between the proposed this regulatory area requirements and existing the Finland Employment Contracts Act obligations should be explicitly addressed in the final rule to prevent redundant compliance efforts.

ACPWB submits that the this regulatory area standard should include periodic review mechanisms allowing organizations to propose refinements based on implementation experience.

Recommendations

  1. The Internal Revenue Service should create a transitory collective bargaining unit determination watch list and increase examination frequency for identified firms.
  2. The Internal Revenue Service should fund the development of open-source compliance-tracking software designed to support organizations in implementing and documenting these compensation requirements compliance.
  3. Establish a fast-track review process for healthcare providers seeking this policy area compliance documentation.
  4. The agency should commit to publishing a comprehensive set of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) and implementation guides at least six months prior to the first compliance deadline.
  5. Establish a employee communications specialists ombudsman role within the Internal Revenue Service to address collective bargaining standards and requirements grievances with maximum resolution time of a transition period of no less than eighteen months.

About This Filing

The American Corporation for Public Well Being (ACPWB) is a nonpartisan research and advisory organization dedicated to advancing workforce equity and compensation transparency. We submit these comments on the Internal Revenue Service's proposed rule regarding collective bargaining unit determination to provide data-driven insights from our extensive work with employers across the United States.
